--- title: "pandas" execute: output: false --- # Quick Reference for Grammar of Data ## select columns ::: {#a51ec45a .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} colleges[['name', 'undergrads']] ``` ::: Documentation on [indexing](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/user_guide/indexing.html) Getting a single column as a `Series`: ::: {#95489cab .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} colleges['name'] ``` ::: Remember: column names are strings (not `colleges[name]`)! ## select rows (`query`) ::: {#1017596c .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} colleges.query("state == 'AK'") ``` ::: Documentation: [pandas.DataFrame.query](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.query.html) ## top and bottom ::: {#4571434b .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} colleges.head(n=2) ``` ::: ::: {#e78cf663 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} colleges.tail(n=3) ``` ::: ## arrange rows (`sort_values`) ::: {#52d4e7fb .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} colleges.sort_values("undergrads").head() ``` ::: ::: {#90720efd .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} colleges.sort_values("undergrads", ascending=False).head() ``` ::: Documentation: [pandas.DataFrame.sort_values](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.sort_values.html) ## counting ::: {#8ad2079d .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} colleges.groupby("state", as_index=False).size() ``` ::: ## grouping / summarizing (general) ::: {#0c634412 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} students_by_state = ( colleges .groupby("state", as_index=False) # <1> .agg(total_undergrads=('undergrads', 'sum')) # <2> .sort_values("total_undergrads", ascending=False) # <3> ) students_by_state ``` ::: 1. Group by state 2. `agg`regate: compute a `total_undergrads` column by (a) extracting the `undergrads` column, and (b) `sum`ming it 3. Sort the result by `total_undergrads` Documentation on [grouping](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/groupby.html). ## grouping by multiple columns ::: {#f5c408e9 .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} ( colleges .groupby(["state", "online_only"], as_index=False) .agg(total_undergrads=('undergrads', 'sum')) ) ``` ::: ## random sampling Shuffle rows: ::: {#e9dbbdd6 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} colleges.sample(frac=1.0).head() ``` ::: Select random rows: ::: {#4c133128 .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} colleges.sample(n=5) ``` ::: ## Deriving new columns ::: {#93163903 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} colleges['named_university'] = colleges['name'].str.contains('University') colleges.groupby('named_university', as_index=False).agg( mean_undergrads=('undergrads', 'mean'), max_undergrads=('undergrads', 'max') ) ``` ::: Note: you can also *chain* these operations using `assign`, which *returns a new `DataFrame`* instead of modifying the original. ::: {#35c14d92 .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} ( colleges .assign(named_university = colleges['name'].str.contains('University')) .groupby('named_university', as_index=False).agg( mean_undergrads=('undergrads', 'mean'), max_undergrads=('undergrads', 'max') ) ) ``` ::: ## `SettingWithCopyWarning` Deriving columns on a subset of rows can cause a warning. For example: ::: {#f0088919 .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} mi_colleges = colleges.query("state == 'MI'") mi_colleges['named_college'] = mi_colleges['name'].str.contains('College') ``` ::: This is pandas trying to keep you from making certain types of mistakes that can be subtle; see the [documentation](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/user_guide/indexing.html#returning-a-view-versus-a-copy). To avoid it, use `assign`: ::: {#1dd36f02 .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} mi_colleges = colleges.query("state == 'MI'") mi_colleges = mi_colleges.assign( named_college = mi_colleges['name'].str.contains('College')) ``` ::: or `.copy`: ::: {#05b52e4b .cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} mi_colleges = colleges.query("state == 'MI'").copy() mi_colleges['named_college'] = mi_colleges['name'].str.contains('College') ``` ::: ## "Broadcast" operations Apply an operation to an entire column at a time. ::: {#6fb820eb .cell execution_count=19} ``` {.python .cell-code} colleges['undergrads'] / 1000 ``` ::: ::: {#2fe13112 .cell execution_count=20} ``` {.python .cell-code} pd.isna(colleges['undergrads']) ``` ::: ## Pairs of columns When broadcasting with a pair of columns, the operation is applied element-wise. ::: {#115f4249 .cell execution_count=21} ``` {.python .cell-code} colleges['city'] + ', ' + colleges['state'] ``` ::: ::: {.callout-note} For more advanced string concatenation, you may want to use `str.cat`: ` ::: {#74d97f58 .cell execution_count=22} ``` {.python .cell-code} colleges['city'].str.cat(colleges['state'], sep=', ') ``` ::: ::: ## Deriving new columns, advanced If you need an operation that isn't built into pandas, you can `apply` your own function. First let's define a function: ::: {#f283d980 .cell execution_count=23} ``` {.python .cell-code} def classify_name(school_name): school_name = school_name.lower() if 'university' in school_name: return 'university' elif 'college' in school_name: return 'college' else: return 'other' # example: classify_name('University of California, Berkeley') ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=23} ``` 'university' ``` ::: ::: Then we `apply` that to each row: ::: {#a1d724e2 .cell execution_count=24} ``` {.python .cell-code} colleges['name_type'] = colleges['name'].apply(classify_name) ``` ::: ::: {#929c6346 .cell execution_count=25} ``` {.python .cell-code} colleges.groupby('name_type', as_index=False).agg( mean_undergrads=('undergrads', 'mean'), max_undergrads=('undergrads', 'max') ) ``` ::: Note: this is slower because it runs unoptimized Python code for each row. First, make it correct, then make it fast (e.g., [`np.select`](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.select.html)). ## Joining (`merge`) If you think you want to: ``` for each row in table A: look up value in table B ``` then you want a join. Example: looking up state names. ::: {#8d81927f .cell execution_count=26} ``` {.python .cell-code} states = pd.read_csv("../static/data/states.csv") states.head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=26} ```{=html}
name postal_code
0 Alabama AL
1 Alaska AK

3 Arkansas AR
4 California CA
``` ::: ::: ::: {#55c51e3e .cell execution_count=27} ``` {.python .cell-code} students_by_state_with_names = ( students_by_state .merge( states, left_on='state', right_on='postal_code', how='left', indicator=True ) ) students_by_state_with_names.head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=27} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ::: {#23bea564 .cell execution_count=28} ``` {.python .cell-code} students_by_state_with_names.tail() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=28} ```{=html}

54 VI 1744.0 U.S. Virgin Islands VI both

56 AS 992.0 American Samoa AS both

58 PW 441.0 NaN NaN left_only
``` ::: ::: ### Join types - **Left join**: use keys from left table - **Right join**: use keys from right table - **Outer join**: use union of both sets of keys - **Inner join**: use *intersection* of both sets of keys See [documentation](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.merge.html) ## Debugging joins Always check your joins! - Check the number of rows in the result - Use `indicator=True` to see which rows came from which table - Use [`validate`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.merge.html) to check that the join is correct. Options: - 'one_to_one' or '1:1': check if merge keys are unique in both left and right datasets. - 'one_to_many' or '1:m': check if merge keys are unique in left dataset. - 'many_to_one' or 'm:1': check if merge keys are unique in right dataset. - 'many_to_many' or 'm:m': allowed, but does not result in checks. **Debugging tool**: Do an `outer` join, then `groupby` your primary key and the `_merge` indicator: ::: {#8be5023e .cell execution_count=29} ``` {.python .cell-code} students_by_state_with_names = ( students_by_state .merge( states, left_on='state', right_on='postal_code', how='outer', indicator=True ) ) ( students_by_state_with_names .groupby(['state', '_merge'], as_index=False) .size() .query("_merge != 'both' and size > 0") ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=29} ```{=html}
state _merge size
33 FM left_only 1
75 MH left_only 1
135 PW left_only 1
``` ::: ::: Things that might be wrong: - You mis-specified the primary key (e.g., it actually should be two columns) - The keys don't match (e.g., one has "US" and the other has "United States") Tools to fix key mismatches: - `replace` to fix a small number of key mismatches - when you have a large number of mismatches, `merge` with a *translation table*, then `fillna` from the translation table. - To make a translation table, you might use fuzzy matching, using tools like [thefuzz](https://github.com/seatgeek/thefuzz) (but be careful) ## Web Scraping You can use [`pd.read_html`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/io.html#io-read-html) to read tables from web pages. This is actually how I made the `states.csv` file that we just read. ::: {#eed11010 .cell execution_count=30} ``` {.python .cell-code} states_tables_raw = pd.read_html("https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_states_and_territories_of_the_United_States", match="postal abbr") print("Found", len(states_tables_raw), "tables") states_tables_raw[-1] ``` ::: Expect the result to be messy. Cleaning it up often requires doing things that are beyond the scope of this class, but here's one example: ::: {#49950eb1 .cell execution_count=31} ``` {.python .cell-code} def clean_states_table(df): return ( df .iloc[:, :2] # we only care about the first two columns .set_axis(['name', 'postal_code'], axis=1) # assign column names .dropna() # drop rows with missing values .assign(name = lambda df: df['name'].str.replace(r'\[.*\]', '')) ) cleaned_territories = clean_states_table(states_tables_raw[-1]) cleaned_territories ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=31} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: This is a good case for using `concat`: ::: {#b1c74442 .cell execution_count=32} ``` {.python .cell-code} state_names = pd.concat([ clean_states_table(table) for table in states_tables_raw ], ignore_index=True) state_names ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=32} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: # Style notes We'll use a consistent `pandas` style in this class. - access columns with `df['col']`, not `df.col` - no index - `groupby` with `as_index=False` - explicit aggregation - `.size` of groups, not `value_counts` Know the rules in order to know when to break them. ## No index - pandas has `index`ing, an unusual concept - not used in SQL, tidyverse, spreadsheets, etc. - even [Ibis](https://ibis-project.org/), next-gen dataframe library by Wes McKinney (pandas creator), doesn't use it. - it's sometimes useful, but often confusing, so we'll avoid it. - so we'll use `as_index=False` in all our `groupby` calls. - so all our aggregation results will be `DataFrames`, not `Series`. ## Explicit aggregation Lazy method: ```python colleges.groupby("state", as_index=False).undergrads.mean() ``` Explicit method: ```python colleges.groupby("state", as_index=False).agg( mean_undergrads=('undergrads', 'mean'), max_undergrads=('undergrads', 'max') ) ``` ## Size of a group Preferred to `value_counts`: - works with multiple columns - returns a `DataFrame`, not a `Series` ::: {.columns} :::: {.column width="50%"} ```python ( colleges .groupby("state", as_index=False) .size() ) ``` ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ```python ( colleges .groupby(["state", "online_only"], as_index=False) .size() ) ``` ::: ::: Compare with `value_counts`: ```python colleges["state"].value_counts() ```
